uncited: Mesh-based initialization converts a polygonal mesh into a set of 3D Gaussian splats to serve as the starting point for optimization or rendering.

It solves the problem of establishing a geometric prior for Gaussian Splatting when a high-quality surface representation is already available, leveraging the explicit nature of Gaussians to support user-guided generation or scene-level inverse rendering.

It differs from sibling methods like [Angle-pose Cuboid Uniform Initialization (ACUI)](4503-angle-pose-cuboid-uniform-initialization-acui.md) by deriving positions from continuous surface geometry rather than volumetric bounding boxes, and from [Learning-based and Generative Initialization](12356-learning-based-and-generative-initialization.md) by relying on deterministic geometric sampling rather than neural priors.
The core mechanism involves sampling points from the surface of an input mesh and assigning Gaussian parameters to these points.
The position of each Gaussian is determined by the sampled surface coordinates.

The orientation and scale are typically aligned with the local surface geometry (e.g., normal-aligned, thin along the normal) to represent the surface as a collection of flat or slightly thickened primitives.
This approach exploits the explicit nature of 3D Gaussian Splatting, allowing for direct integration with existing mesh processing pipelines.
Mesh-based initialization has emerged as a critical component in advanced Gaussian Splatting applications where geometric priors are valuable.
The approach allows for the integration of traditional computer graphics assets (meshes) with differentiable rendering frameworks, enabling hybrid workflows.
